title: Infra GPU Fleet, Capacity, Cloud Accounts & CI/CD Playbook (2026 updates)
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Summary

This playbook consolidates infrastructure engineering guidance for Redwood's GPU fleet and capacity planning, cloud accounts and networking, Terraform/IaC module standards, and CI/CD build pipelines. It is intended for infra engineers, SREs, and platform owners responsible for provisioning, scaling, and operating GPU-backed inference clusters across cloud regions and Dedicated/Private deployments.

Scope

- GPU fleet sizing and capacity model for production inference services (hosted + dedicated)
- Cloud account layout, networking best practices (VPCs, peering, transit, egress controls)
- Terraform module interface and IaC patterns (reusable modules, inputs/outputs, versioning)
- CI/CD pipelines for infra changes (plan/review/apply guardrails, testing on staging)
- Operational runbooks for capacity incidents, scaling events, and maintenance windows

Ownership

- Primary owner: infra-platform team (engineers: @infra-platform)
- SLA/operational owner: eng-sre oncall rotation
- Terraform module maintainers: infra-iac subteam

Architecture overview

- Services: gpu-scheduler (internal), capacity-controller (k8s-controller), instance-provisioner (cloud automation), vpc-router (networking), monitoring-agent
- Regions: us-west-2 (primary), us-east-1 (warm), eu-west-1 (replica for EU customers)
- Account topology: 1 management account (billing + shared services), per-region infra accounts for compute, per-customer dedicated accounts when required by contract

Capacity model (summary)

- Target latency SLOs (p50/p95/p99) are set at the service level; capacity planning uses p95 token/sec trends.
- Headroom policy: maintain 20% spare GPU capacity during business hours, 40% spare during major launch windows.
- Scale triggers:
  - Autoscale up: sustained utilization > 70% across GPU pool for 10 minutes
  - Autoscale down: sustained utilization < 35% for 30 minutes and queue length < 5
- Capacity units: use "GPU slots" (one slot = 80GB A100 equivalent vGPU allocation). Convert other instance types to slots via the GPU equivalency table in the Reference section.

Cloud accounts & networking

Guidelines:
- Management account contains Terraform state backend, shared DNS, IAM role bastions, and central logging.
- Each region has a dedicated infra account with: compute subnets, bastion endpoints, NAT/egress, and transit gateway attachments.
- Customer Dedicated deployments get separate accounts and isolated VPCs with restricted cross-account access via assumed roles and restricted peering.
- Use AWS Transit Gateway (or equivalent) for multi-VPC routing; prefer route table per environment (prod/staging).
- Egress control: enforce HTTP proxy for external outbound connections; restrict world-accessible endpoints except for approved image registries and artifact stores.

Networking checklist (minimum):
- CIDR allocation plan documented and reserve ranges for future expansions
- Subnet tagging: environment, availability-zone, purpose, team-owned
- NACLs for public subnets; security groups are primary enforcement for instances
- Flow logs enabled to central logging bucket with lifecycle 90 days

Terraform / IaC module standards

Principles:
- Modules are versioned (semver) and published to the private module registry.
- Keep modules small and composable: network, compute, iam, monitoring, bootstrap
- All modules must include: inputs list, outputs list, example usage, and a CHANGELOG.md
- Prevent drift with terraform fmt, terraform validate, and policy checks in CI (OPA/Conftest or Sentinel)

Required module interface examples:

Network module (example inputs/outputs):
- Inputs: vpc_cidr, public_subnets, private_subnets, tags
- Outputs: vpc_id, public_route_table_ids, private_route_table_ids, subnet_ids

Compute module usage example (Terraform HCL):
```terraform
module "gpu_node_group" {
  source          = "git::ssh://git@repo.redwood.internal/infra/modules//compute/gpu?ref=v1.3.0"
  name            = "inference-gpu-pool-${var.env}"
  instance_type   = "p4d.24xlarge"
  desired_count   = 12
  min_count       = 4
  max_count       = 48
  ssh_key_name    = var.ssh_key_name
  subnet_ids      = module.network.private_subnet_ids
  tags = merge(var.common_tags, { "role" = "gpu-inference" })
}
```

State & secrets:
- Remote state stored in the management account S3 with KMS encryption and state locking via DynamoDB
- Secrets accessed by modules via a dedicated secrets module that reads from the central KMS-backed secret store; do not hard-code keys in modules

CI/CD and build pipelines

Pipeline goals:
- Ensure every Terraform change is peer-reviewed and validated by plan outputs and policy checks before apply
- Run automated integration tests against a short-lived staging environment for high-risk changes (networking, IAM)
- Enforce signed commits and branch protections on infra repos

Recommended pipeline steps (example GitHub Actions / Jenkins):
1. PR created: run terraform fmt/validate + tflint + unit tests on helper scripts
2. Plan stage: create terraform plan and publish an artifact (plan file) to PR comment with human-readable summary
3. Policy checks: run OPA/Conftest against plan; fail on high-severity violations (open network, public S3, missing encryption)
4. Multi-approver gate: require 2 approvers for changes that touch network or IAM; 1 approver for compute scaling less than 20%
5. Apply: apply is performed by the infra deployment bot role after merge and successful scheduled window or manual trigger for prod

CI tips:
- Use ephemeral test accounts for integration tests and tear them down after validation
- Cache provider plugins in CI runner for faster builds

Runbooks and operational procedures

1) GPU capacity incident (high queue & exhausted slots)

- Symptoms: inference request queue length rises > 1000, p95 latency doubles, GPU pool utilization > 90% and autoscaler not triggering new nodes
- Immediate steps:
  1. Notify oncall via PagerDuty channel "infra-gpu-capacity"
  2. Confirm autoscaler logs: kubectl -n gpu get hpa/gpu-worker -o yaml or check capacity-controller logs in CloudWatch/Logging UI
  3. If autoscaler failed: check IAM role for instance provisioning, check quota limits in the cloud account ("service-quotas")
  4. Temporarily increase desired_count via CI/CD apply to add 6 slots if autoscale is unhealthy (follow emergency change checklist)
  5. Engage cloud provider support if we hit hard quota limits (provide support ticket template in Appendix)
  6. Post-incident: run capacity analysis, add pre-warming policy or increase baseline pool for upcoming launches

2) Scaling rollback / failed bootstrap

- Symptoms: new nodes join but kubelet fails to register or pods crash on image pull
- Steps:
  1. Check instance boot logs via cloud console and ssh into a node (if allowed)
  2. Check user-data / cloud-init failures and bootstrap errors in the cloud-init log (/var/log/cloud-init.log)
  3. If image pull failure: verify ECR/GCR permissions and image tag; temporarily roll nodes using older working AMI
  4. If kubelet registration failing: drain node and mark for reprovision, run kubeadm reset (if self-managed) or replace node pool

Monitoring, SLOs & alerts

SLOs (example):
- Inference service p95 latency < 500ms (objective)
- Request success rate >= 99.9% per day
- Infrastructure availability (node pool ready) >= 99.95% monthly

Key alerts (examples):
- gpu_pool_utilization_high: when GPU utilization > 85% for 5 minutes (Severity P1)
- autoscaler_failed: when node provisioning API returns 5xx or user quota errors (Severity P1)
- image_registry_unreachable: when image pull failures > 5% of pod starts (Severity P2)
- flow_logs_missing: if VPC flow logs are not publishing to central bucket for > 1 hour (Severity P2)

Alert actions should reference runbook sections by ID and include runbook links in the alert payload for the oncall engineer.

Operational windows and maintenance

- Regular maintenance windows: Sundays 02:00-06:00 UTC for non-critical infra changes; emergency changes use the emergency_change checklist below
- Database and central services maintenance require a separate communications plan and 72-hour notice to downstream teams

Change & release management

- Use canary deploys for large fleet changes: roll 5% -> 25% -> 100% with 30-minute observation windows
- All prod-affecting changes require a runbook and rollback plan in the PR description
- Emergency change process:
  1. Triage and impact assessment (owner documents reason and risk)
  2. Get a mitigating approver (SRE lead or infra director)
  3. Apply change with a post-change validation checklist (smoke tests)
  4. Communicate on #infra-updates and update the change log

Appendices

A. Quota & support ticket template (cloud provider)
- Subject: "Urgent: GPU quota increase request for Redwood Inference - account <account-id>"
- Body: include region, resource (GPUs, vCPUs), current usage, requested limit, impact description, and ticket priority

B. Terraform module checklist (pre-merge):
- terraform fmt passes
- terraform validate passes
- module has README, Inputs and Outputs documented
- module has unit tests / policy checks

C. Useful commands
- Check GPU pool utilization: kubectl -n gpu top nodes | grep -i gpu
- Check autoscaler logs: aws logs tail /aws/eks/gpu/cluster --since 2h --follow
- Force scale via infra deployment bot (CLI): infra-deploy apply --env prod --module compute/gpu --var desired_count=18 --reason "emergency scale"

References
